expectations.description: Recommends polychoric correlations (cor='poly' argument or similar)
expectations.evidence: Uses cor='poly' in both fa.parallel() and fa() calls, with explanation: 'Likert items are ordinal, not continuous. Pearson correlations applied to 5-point scales underestimate the true latent correlations.'

expectations.description: Recommends oblique rotation (oblimin or promax) rather than varimax
expectations.evidence: Uses rotate='oblimin' with reasoning: 'Psychological constructs are almost always correlated. Using varimax or another orthogonal rotation imposes the constraint that your factors are uncorrelated — a constraint that is rarely true.' Promax mentioned as alternative.

expectations.description: Provides a code example with fa() and reasonable arguments
expectations.evidence: Full fa() code block with nfactors, fm='minres', rotate='oblimin', cor='poly', and inline comments. Also includes fa.parallel() code block.

expectations.description: Mentions parallel analysis (fa.parallel) for determining factor count before running fa()
expectations.evidence: Step 1 is entirely dedicated to parallel analysis with fa.parallel(your_data, fa='fa', cor='poly'), called 'more reliable than Kaiser's eigenvalue > 1 rule.'

expectations.description: Mentions an extraction method (minres or ml) with brief justification
expectations.evidence: Recommends fm='minres' with justification: 'minimizes the off-diagonal residuals without requiring multivariate normality... less prone to Heywood cases compared to maximum likelihood.' Also notes when ml is appropriate.

expectations.description: Does not default to varimax rotation
expectations.evidence: Uses oblimin, and explicitly states: 'Do not use varimax by default for psychological scale data.'

expectations.description: Does not default to Pearson correlations for Likert data without flagging it
expectations.evidence: Uses cor='poly' throughout. Explicitly warns against Pearson: 'Pearson correlations applied to 5-point scales underestimate the true latent correlations, which biases your loadings downward and can distort factor structure.'
